_comment: Rules that read the code rather than the text of it. Each carries one tree-sitter query per language, so teaching a rule about another language is an entry here rather than a change in Rust. What a query cannot express is judgement — whether the argument is a literal, which decides between an ugly call and a dangerous one — and that lives in ast.rs where it can be tested. Captures: @hit is what gets reported, @arg is the argument judged for literalness.

rules.title: Code is built at run time and executed
rules.description: A value decided while the app is running is handed to something that executes it as code.
rules.impact: If any part of that value can be influenced from outside, whoever influences it chooses what the app does next.
rules.fix: Work out what the code is actually for. A lookup table, a match on a fixed set of names, or a small parser will do the job without running text as code.

safeArgumentPatterns.shell: ^"?\$\((ssh-agent|brew shellenv|pyenv init|rbenv init|nodenv init|direnv hook|opam env|conda shell)[^$`]*\)"?$

nothingToFind.c: C has no way to run a string as C. A shell command is the shell-command rule's, and an embedded interpreter such as Lua is not looked for.
nothingToFind.go: Go has no built-in way to run a string as code. An embedded interpreter such as yaegi would be one, and is not looked for.
nothingToFind.rust: Rust has no built-in way to run a string as code. An embedded interpreter such as rhai would be one, and is not looked for.

rules.title: A shell command is built from a value
rules.description: A command line is assembled from something other than fixed text and handed to the shell.
rules.impact: A semicolon or a backtick in the wrong place turns one command into two, and the second one is whatever the attacker wanted.
rules.fix: Pass the program and its arguments as a list instead of a string, so the shell never parses them. Where a shell is genuinely needed, validate the value against a fixed set first.

queries.python:
[(call function: (attribute object: (identifier) @mod attribute: (identifier) @fn)
              arguments: (argument_list . (_) @arg))
       (call function: (identifier) @fn arguments: (argument_list . (_) @arg))] @hit
queries.dart:
[(call_expression function: (member_expression object: (identifier) @mod property: (identifier) @fn)
                 arguments: (arguments . (_) @arg))
 (call_expression function: (member_expression object: (identifier) @mod property: (identifier))
                  arguments: (arguments . (string_literal) @fn . (list_literal) @arg))] @hit
queries.swift:
[(call_expression (simple_identifier) @fn @mod (call_suffix (value_arguments . (value_argument) @arg)))
 (assignment target: (directly_assignable_expression (navigation_expression suffix: (navigation_suffix suffix: (simple_identifier) @mod)))
             result: (array_literal . element: (line_string_literal) @fn) @arg)
 (value_argument name: (value_argument_label (simple_identifier) @mod)
                 value: (array_literal . element: (line_string_literal) @fn) @arg)] @hit
queries.go:
[(call_expression function: (selector_expression operand: (identifier) @mod field: (field_identifier) @fn)
                  arguments: (argument_list . (_) @arg))
 (call_expression function: (selector_expression operand: (identifier) @mod field: (field_identifier))
                  arguments: (argument_list . (interpreted_string_literal) @fn . (_) . (_) @arg))
 (call_expression function: (selector_expression operand: (identifier) @mod field: (field_identifier))
                  arguments: (argument_list . (_) . (interpreted_string_literal) @fn . (_) . (_) @arg))] @hit
queries.rust:
[(call_expression function: (scoped_identifier path: (_) @mod name: (identifier) @fn)
                  arguments: (arguments . (_) @arg))
 (call_expression function: (field_expression value: (call_expression function: (field_expression value: (call_expression function: (scoped_identifier path: (_) @mod) arguments: (arguments . (string_literal) @fn)))
                                                                           arguments: (arguments . (string_literal))))
                  arguments: (arguments . (_) @arg))
 (call_expression function: (field_expression value: (call_expression function: (scoped_identifier path: (_) @mod) arguments: (arguments . (string_literal) @fn)))
                  arguments: (arguments . [(array_expression) @arg (reference_expression value: (array_expression) @arg)]))] @hit

rules.title: A database query is built by joining text together
rules.description: A query is assembled from pieces rather than sent with its values kept separate.
rules.impact: A quote in someone's name is enough to change what the query does, and a deliberate one can read or delete any table the app can reach.
rules.fix: Send the query with placeholders and pass the values alongside it. Every database library supports this, and it is shorter than building the string.

rules.title: Data from outside is turned back into objects unsafely
rules.description: A format that can describe arbitrary objects is being read with the reader that builds them.
rules.impact: Reading the data is enough to run code: the attacker does not need the app to use the result, only to load it.
rules.fix: Use the safe reader — yaml.safe_load rather than yaml.load — and prefer a format that carries data only, such as JSON, for anything that arrives from outside.

nothingToFind.c: C has no object deserializer. Reading bytes into a struct is a memory-safety question, which this rule does not ask.
nothingToFind.dart: Dart's decoders, jsonDecode among them, give back maps and lists; no library call in common use builds whatever object the data names.
nothingToFind.go: Go's decoders (encoding/json, encoding/gob, encoding/xml) fill in a type the program names; none of them builds whatever type the data asks for.
nothingToFind.rust: serde fills in a type the program names; no deserializer in common use builds whatever type the data asks for.
nothingToFind.shell: A shell script has no objects to deserialize; it passes text between programs.

rules.title: A command is run with backticks, built from text
rules.description: Backticks run a shell command and hand back its output. This one is assembled from pieces rather than written out.
rules.impact: Whatever ends up inside the backticks is run by a shell, so a semicolon in someone's input starts a second command with the app's own permissions.
rules.fix: Run the program directly with its arguments as a list, rather than building one string for a shell to pull apart.

nothingToFind.go: Backticks in Go make a raw string, not a command.
nothingToFind.javascript: Backticks in JavaScript make a template string, not a command; a command is the shell-command rule's.
nothingToFind.kotlin: Backticks in Kotlin quote a name, not a command.
nothingToFind.shell: In a shell script backticks are command substitution, the ordinary way to use a command's output; a command built from a value is the shell-command rule's (`sh -c`).
nothingToFind.swift: Backticks in Swift quote a name, not a command.
nothingToFind.typescript: Backticks in TypeScript make a template string, not a command; a command is the shell-command rule's.

rules.title: A file is opened at a path built from a value
rules.description: A file path used to read, write or delete a file is built from a value rather than written out, so the file operation goes wherever that value points.
rules.impact: If any part of the path comes from a request, a name like ../../etc/passwd reads or overwrites a file outside the folder the app meant to use.
rules.fix: Keep user-submitted file names out of file paths: store files under names the app generates, and look them up by id. Where a submitted name has to be used, reduce it to a bare name (secure_filename in Flask, path.basename in Node) and check that the resolved path is still inside the folder it should be in.

rules.title: A disallowed hash function is used
rules.description: MD5 or SHA-1 is used as a hash function. Both have practical collision attacks, and approved-hash rules disallow them for any cryptographic use.
rules.impact: Anything that relies on the hash to tell two things apart, or to prove something was not changed, can be fooled by somebody who builds a second input with the same hash. Used for passwords, both are also fast enough to guess through quickly.
rules.fix: Use SHA-256 or stronger for integrity and signatures, and a password hashing function (Argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt) for passwords. If this hash is only a cache key or a file checksum with no security purpose, say so where it is used; Python lets you pass usedforsecurity=False.

queries.swift:
[(call_expression (navigation_expression target: (navigation_expression suffix: (navigation_suffix suffix: (simple_identifier) @mod))
                                      suffix: (navigation_suffix suffix: (simple_identifier) @fn)))
 (call_expression (navigation_expression target: (simple_identifier) @mod
                                      suffix: (navigation_suffix suffix: (simple_identifier) @fn)))
 (call_expression (simple_identifier) @fn @mod)] @hit

rules.title: A cipher or block mode that is not approved is used
rules.description: Data is encrypted with ECB, the block mode that encrypts equal blocks to equal output, or with a retired cipher such as DES, triple DES, RC4, RC2 or Blowfish.
rules.impact: ECB leaves the shape of the data visible through the encryption, and the retired ciphers can be broken or have known practical attacks, so the encrypted data is less private than it looks.
rules.fix: Use AES with GCM (or ChaCha20-Poly1305) through your language's high-level library, which chooses the mode and the nonce for you. In Java, always name the mode: Cipher.getInstance("AES") quietly means ECB.

rules.title: The app redirects to a destination built from a value
rules.description: A redirect sends the user to a destination that is built from a value rather than written out or produced from the app's own routes.
rules.impact: If the destination comes from the request, as a ?next= parameter usually does, a link on the app's own domain can send somebody to a lookalike sign-in page on another domain, and the address they clicked was genuine.
rules.fix: Redirect only to the app's own routes, built with its router (url_for, reverse, a Rails _path helper), or check the destination against a short list of allowed hosts. For a return-to address, accept only a path that starts with a single / and not //.

rules.title: Code downloaded from the network is run straight away
rules.description: A script downloads a third-party component and hands it to a shell or an interpreter as it arrives, so it runs whatever the address serves, with nothing checking it came from the expected repository or is the version meant.
rules.impact: Whoever controls that address, or anything between it and the machine, chooses what runs, with the permissions of the script, often root.
rules.fix: Download to a file, check it against a published checksum or signature, then run it. Better still, install the tool from the system's package manager, or pin a version in a lockfile.

queries.shell:
[(pipeline (command name: (command_name) @mod) (command name: (command_name) @fn))
 (pipeline (command name: (command_name) @mod) (command name: (command_name) . argument: (word) @fn))
 (command name: (command_name) @fn argument: (process_substitution (command name: (command_name) @mod)))] @hit
